# Heat Pump Dryer

## Setup

I run a 9 kg heat-pump unit in the utility corner, standing on a rubber mat. The mat matters more than I expected when I bought it. It deadens the hum of the compressor and stops the cabinet creeping across the tiles on a long run. The drum on this kind of machine never gets properly hot. It sits near 60 C for most of a cycle. That is why the clothes come out warm rather than baked, and why a full drum takes about two hours twenty instead of the fifty minutes the old vented unit managed. The condensate leaves by one of two routes. I can let it collect in the tank at the top left and carry that to the sink, or I can push the hose into the standpipe beside the laundry sink. I used the drain hose for the first year and then went back to the tank, because the hose has to rise 60 cm to reach the standpipe here and anything less than a clean, gentle arc lets water pool in the run. The unit wants a firm level floor and about 5 cm of clearance behind it so the air can move.

## Cleaning

The fluff filter sits behind the plinth door and comes out every second load. I pull the drawer, peel the mat of fibre off the screen and rinse both parts under the tap until the water runs clear, then stand them on the draining board to dry before they go back. It takes a minute and it is the single thing that keeps the run time steady. The fine mat is the part that matters; when it is furred, the cycle stretches by twenty minutes and the clothes come out hotter than they should. The condenser fins get a rinse under the tap every three months. I unclip the lower cover, lift the fin block free on the model that allows it, and hose the grey felt off the plates from the back so the fibre goes down the sink rather than into the gaps between the fins. The water runs grey for the first ten seconds and then clears. The drum gets a wipe with a damp cloth when the cabinet is done, and the cabinet takes the same cloth while I am there. I never polish the plastic front, since polish smears and shows every finger mark. I leave the door ajar between loads so the inside airs, and I do not put anything in the drum to mask a smell; if the drum smells, the fins need the rinse.

## Maintenance

Once a month I empty the tank, wipe the cabinet and the door face, and check that the machine still sits level. I put a spirit level across the top and turn the front feet a quarter turn if it has drifted, which it does after a heavy load of towels. I check the mat has not walked out from under a corner, latch the condenser cover, and look at the door catch to see the striker still meets the housing square. If the hose is in use I run a thumb along the first metre of it to feel for a flat spot. I also count the cycles on the dial and note the number in the folder with the manual, because the run time creeps up slowly and I want to see it coming.

The tank gets a rinse, not just an empty. Warm water and a drop of washing-up liquid, swilled round the inside, then left upside down to dry. At the three-month mark I found a slimy film along the inner seam where the condensate had sat, and since then it gets the rinse every time it comes out rather than once in a while. If I forget for a fortnight, the water in the bottom goes cloudy and smells faintly of the drain, which is enough warning for me.

The door seal is a soft rubber lip running right round the opening. I wipe the fold with a damp cloth once a month and run a finger round behind it to feel for grit, because a grain of sand trapped in the lip will mark the drum edge and let warm air out. At month five I felt a roughness on the lower run of the seal and found a length of dental floss wound into the fold, left in a pocket by one of the children. It came out with a tug and the seal sat flat again. I dry it afterwards rather than leaving it damp, since a wet fold grows a black speckle over a summer.

The filter housing behind the plinth door needs more than the filter itself. The fluff filter here is a two-part job, a coarse screen and a finer mat behind it, and both get rinsed every second load in warm water until the water runs clear. The housing itself is a plastic throat that the fluff rides through on its way to the condenser, and every few months I take a vacuum nozzle to the corners of it, because a ridge of compacted fibre builds up along the inner lip where my fingers cannot reach. At the six-month check the ridge was about 4 mm deep and felt like felt board. Clearing it took the cycle time from two hours fifty back to two hours twenty, though I could not say whether the throat or the fins did most of the work.

The compressor grille is at the back, low down, a slatted cover over the sealed unit. Dust and laundry fibre coat the slats from the room side. I brush it with the soft attachment on the vacuum every three months. At the eight-month mark the grille was uniformly grey and the machine ran noticeably warmer down the back, and the compressor note went from a soft hum to a harder tone on the last half hour of a cycle. A quick brush restored the quieter note within a day or two. The compressor has no serviceable parts in it and I have never touched the pipework.

The airflow path runs from the drum, through the fluff filter, across the evaporator fins at the front, over the condenser behind and back into the drum. The evaporator is the cold side and it is where the water is wrung out of the air, so it collects a mat of fibre on the fin edges even with a clean filter. That is why the fins get their rinse: the water sheet off the tap lifts the fibre off the plates, and I can see the grey water run out of the housing when I tip it. At the twelve-month check the fins had a felt layer across the first third of the face and the machine took two hours forty to dry a mixed load it had managed in two hours ten when new. The cycle count now sits around four hundred and the run time has stayed steady since the fins were cleaned.

The drain hose has been the recurring nuisance. It needs to rise 60 cm to the standpipe, and it must have no dip anywhere along that rise. The first winter I had it lying in a gentle loop behind the machine and the machine gurgled at the start of every cycle, then shut down with water in the base tray, about a litre of it, which I mopped out. The loop held a slug of water that the pump could lift at the start but not push past once it had grown. I re-clipped the run to the wall so it climbs steadily and never sags. Since then the condensate goes out cleanly and the tray stays dry, and the only water I handle is what the tank catches when I use that instead. With the hose sitting at the right height and the drum holding near 60 C, a mixed load now comes out dry in about two hours twenty with no damp corners.

## Troubleshooting

If a load comes out damp at the end of a full cycle, the odds are the drain hose is rising too high above the standpipe or has a dip that holds water, so the machine trips out before the run finishes and leaves the clothes sitting wet in a warm drum. The second thing I check is the fluff filter, since a matted screen throttles the path just as badly and takes a minute to rule out. I look at the position of the hose first because it is the fault that comes back if I have moved the machine for any reason. A panel code that will not clear usually resets if I switch the unit off at the wall for a minute and start it again, and the code on this model relates to the condensate pump rather than the heater. A drum that turns but stays cold points at the compressor or the refrigerant circuit, and that is a call to the engineer rather than something I can fix at home. A loud rattle on start up is usually a coin or a hair grip that has made it past the filter and is sitting in the fan housing.
